text:
“You are young, you are beautiful; life will console you. You are noble, and the memory of a good deed will redeem many things from the past for you. In the six months he has known you, Armand has forgotten me. Four times I have written to him without his once thinking of answering me. I could have died without his knowing it!

“Whatever your resolve to live differently from the way you have lived, Armand, who loves you, will not consent to the seclusion to which his modest position would condemn you, and which is not suited to your beauty. Who knows what he might then do! He has gambled; I found out. Without your telling me anything about it, I know it still; but, in a moment of intoxication, he might have lost part of what I have been amassing for many years for my daughter’s dowry, for him, and for the peace of my old age. What might have happened may still happen.

“Are you certain, moreover, that the life you would leave for him would not attract you again? Are you certain, you who have loved him, that you will not love another? Will you not, in the end, suffer from the obstacles your relationship will place in your lover’s life, and for which you may be unable to console him if, with age, thoughts of ambition succeed dreams of love? Reflect on all this, madame: you love Armand; prove it to him by the only means still left to you of proving it to him—by sacrificing your love to his future. No misfortune has yet occurred, but misfortunes would occur, and perhaps greater ones than those I foresee. Armand may become jealous of a man who has loved you; he may challenge him, he may fight, he may finally be killed; and think what you would suffer before the father who would demand an accounting from you for his son’s life.

“Lastly, my child, know everything, for I have not told you everything; know, then, what brought me to Paris. I have a daughter, as I have just told you, young, beautiful, pure as an angel. She is in love, and she too has made that love the dream of her life. I had written all this to Armand, but, wholly absorbed in you, he did not answer me. Well, my daughter is going to marry. She is marrying the man she loves; she is entering an honorable family that wants everything in mine to be honorable. The family of the man who is to become my son-in-law has learned how Armand lives in Paris and has declared to me that it will withdraw its word if Armand continues this life. The future of a girl who has done you no harm, and who has the right to count on the future, is in your hands.

“Have you the right, and do you feel you have the strength, to shatter it? In the name of your love and your repentance, Marguerite, grant me my daughter’s happiness.

“I wept silently, my friend, before all these reflections, which I had often made myself and which, in your father’s mouth, acquired an even graver reality. I told myself everything your father did not dare tell me and which had come to his lips twenty times: that, after all, I was nothing but a kept woman, and that whatever reason I might give for our relationship, it would always have the appearance of a calculation; that my past life left me no right to dream of such a future, and that I was accepting responsibilities for which my habits and my reputation afforded no guarantee. Lastly, I loved you, Armand. The paternal manner in which Monsieur Duval spoke to me, the chaste sentiments he evoked in me, the esteem of that loyal old man which I was about to win, and yours, which I was certain of having later—all this awakened noble thoughts in my heart that raised me in my own eyes and gave voice to holy vanities until then unknown to me. When I thought that one day this old man, who was imploring me for his son’s future, would tell his daughter to mingle my name with her prayers, like the name of a mysterious friend, I was transformed, and I was proud of myself.

“The exaltation of the moment perhaps exaggerated the truth of these impressions; but that is what I felt, my friend, and these new feelings silenced the counsels given me by the memory of the happy days spent with you.”

“—Very well, monsieur, I said to your father as I wiped away my tears. Do you believe that I love your son?

“—Yes, Monsieur Duval said to me.

“—With a selfless love?

“—Yes.

“—Do you believe that I had made this love the hope, the dream, and the pardon of my life?

“—Firmly.

“—Well, monsieur, embrace me once as you would embrace your daughter, and I swear to you that this kiss, the only truly chaste one I have ever received, will make me strong against my love, and that within a week your son will have returned to you, perhaps unhappy for a time, but cured forever.

“—You are a noble girl, your father replied, kissing me on the forehead, and you are attempting something for which God will give you credit; but I greatly fear that you will achieve nothing with my son.

“—Oh! Do not worry, monsieur; he will hate me.

“There had to be an insurmountable barrier between us, for one as well as for the other.

“I wrote to Prudence that I accepted Monsieur le Comte de N…’s proposals, and that she should go and tell him that I would have supper with her and with him.

“I sealed the letter and, without telling him what it contained, asked your father to have it delivered to its address upon arriving in Paris.

“He nevertheless asked me what it contained.

“—It is your son’s happiness, I answered him.

“Your father embraced me one last time. I felt on my forehead two tears of gratitude that were like the baptism of my former sins, and at the very moment when I had just consented to give myself to another man, I shone with pride at the thought of what I was redeeming through this new sin.

“It was only natural, Armand; you had told me that your father was the most honorable man one could ever meet.

“Monsieur Duval got back into his carriage and left.

“But I was a woman, and when I saw you again, I could not keep from weeping; yet I did not weaken.

“Did I do right? That is what I ask myself today, as I take, ill, to a bed that I may leave only when dead.

“You witnessed what I felt as the hour of our inevitable separation drew nearer; your father was no longer there to sustain me, and there was a moment when I came very close to confessing everything to you, so terrified was I by the thought that you were going to hate and despise me.
